decks.title: Minerals and Energy Resources — Part 1: Minerals
goals: Explain how minerals occur in igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks, placers and ocean waters
Classify minerals as ferrous, non-ferrous and non-metallic, with uses
Name the main iron-ore, manganese, copper, bauxite and mica areas and locate key mines
Explain why minerals must be conserved and suggest methods

slides.heading: Minerals and Energy Resources
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what minerals are, where they hide in the rocks, where India mines them, and why they will not last for ever.

visual.alt: Overview of Part 1: what a mineral is, how minerals occur, ferrous minerals, non-ferrous and non-metallic minerals, and conservation
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Namaste! Look around you. The steel in your school gate, the copper in the wires, the cement in the walls and the salt in your food all began as minerals in the Earth. In this part we learn how minerals form, where India mines them, and why we must use them carefully, because once they are gone, they are gone.

slides.heading: Minerals, rocks and ores
slides.body_md: A **mineral** is a naturally formed substance with a uniform make-up and a definite internal structure. **Rocks** are combinations of minerals; a few, such as **limestone**, are made of one. An **ore** is a mineral mixed with other elements, concentrated enough to be worth mining.

nodes.label: Concentrated in some places as ores

visual.alt: Flow: minerals combine to form rocks; in some places they are concentrated as ores; ores are mined if extraction pays

slides.narration: Three words to keep apart. A mineral is a natural substance with a definite structure. A rock is usually a mixture of minerals. And an ore is a deposit where a useful mineral is concentrated enough to make mining profitable. The same metal scattered thinly through ordinary rock is not an ore, because digging it out would cost more than it is worth.

slides.heading: Five ways minerals occur

rows: Molten or gaseous material cools in cracks of igneous and metamorphic rocks
Deposition and concentration in sedimentary rocks; evaporation in dry areas
Coal, some iron ore; gypsum, potash, sodium salt
Weathering removes soluble parts, leaving the ore
Water-resistant minerals collect in sands of valleys and hill bases
Dissolved in sea water or as nodules on the floor
Common salt, magnesium, bromine; manganese nodules

visual.alt: Table of five modes of occurrence: veins and lodes such as copper; beds or layers such as coal and gypsum; residual deposits such as bauxite; placers such as gold; and ocean waters and beds such as salt and manganese nodules

slides.narration: Minerals hide in the Earth in five main ways. Molten material cooling in cracks forms veins and lodes, the home of tin and copper. Sedimentary layers hold coal and, where water evaporates, salts like gypsum. Weathering leaves bauxite behind. River sands collect gold and platinum as placers. And the sea gives us salt, magnesium and bromine.

slides.heading: Quick check: veins and lodes
slides.narration: Small ones are veins. What are the big ones called?

slides.heading: Where in India are the minerals?
bullets: The old rocks of the **peninsula** hold most of India's **coal**, metallic minerals and **mica**.
Sedimentary rocks on the western and eastern flanks, in **Gujarat** and **Assam**, hold most of the **petroleum**.
**Rajasthan** has many **non-ferrous** minerals.
The **northern alluvial plains** have almost **no** economic minerals.
In Meghalaya, **rat-hole mining** of coal by families has been declared **illegal** by the National Green Tribunal.

visual.alt: Table: the peninsular plateau has coal, metallic minerals and mica; Gujarat and Assam have petroleum; Rajasthan has non-ferrous minerals; the northern plains have almost none

slides.narration: India's minerals are unevenly spread. The ancient rocks of the peninsula are a treasure house of coal, iron, manganese and mica. Petroleum lies in sedimentary rocks of Gujarat and Assam. Rajasthan has many non-ferrous minerals. But the great northern plains, built of young river silt, have almost none. Geology decides where mines can exist.

slides.heading: Classifying minerals

nodes.label: Non-metallic: mica, salt, potash, sulphur, granite, limestone, marble, sandstone
Ferrous: iron ore, manganese, nickel, cobalt

visual.alt: Tree: minerals are metallic, non-metallic or energy minerals; metallic minerals are ferrous such as iron ore and manganese, non-ferrous such as copper and bauxite, or precious such as gold

slides.narration: Here is the family tree of minerals. Metallic minerals split into ferrous ones that contain iron, like iron ore and manganese; non-ferrous ones like copper and bauxite; and precious ones like gold. Non-metallic minerals include mica and limestone. Energy minerals are coal, petroleum and gas. Ferrous minerals account for about three-quarters of the value of metallic minerals produced in India.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: classify from clues
slides.body_md: Task: *Classify each mineral and give one use: (i) a metal that is malleable, ductile and conducts well; (ii) a mineral that splits into thin insulating sheets; (iii) an ore with up to 70 per cent iron.*
bullets: Step 1 — (i) Clues: malleable, ductile, conductor → **copper**, non-ferrous; use: electric cables.
Step 2 — (ii) Clues: thin sheets, insulator → **mica**, non-metallic; use: electrical and electronic goods.
Step 3 — (iii) Clue: up to 70 per cent iron → **magnetite**, ferrous; use: steel and the electrical industry.
Step 4 — Write class and use for each; examiners give a mark for each correct pair.

visual.alt: Table: malleable, ductile conductor is copper, non-ferrous, used in cables; thin insulating sheets is mica, non-metallic, used in electronics; up to 70 per cent iron is magnetite, ferrous, used for steel

slides.narration: Clue questions test whether you understand properties, not just names. Malleable, ductile and a good conductor? That is copper. Thin sheets that insulate? Mica. Seventy per cent iron? Magnetite. For each, write the mineral, its class and one use. Three neat pairs, three marks.

slides.heading: Iron ore: the base of heavy industry

rows: Very high-grade hematite; exported via Visakhapatnam
Kudremukh developed as a 100 per cent export unit; slurry pipeline towards Mangaluru
Lower-grade ore, efficiently mined; exported via Marmagao

visual.alt: Table of iron-ore belts: Odisha–Jharkhand with Badampahar, Gua and Noamundi; Durg–Bastar–Chandrapur with the Bailadila hills, exported via Visakhapatnam; the Karnataka belt with Ballari and Kudremukh; and the Maharashtra–Goa belt exported via Marmagao

slides.narration: Almost every machine begins as iron, and India has plenty of good ore. Magnetite is the richest, with up to seventy per cent iron. Hematite is used in the largest amounts. Learn four belts: Odisha and Jharkhand, Durg and Bastar with the famous Bailadila hills, the Karnataka belt with Ballari and Kudremukh, and the Maharashtra–Goa belt that exports through Marmagao.

slides.heading: Quick check: the richest ore
slides.narration: Which ore has the most iron, and is also strongly magnetic?

slides.heading: Manganese, copper and bauxite

rows: About 10 kg per tonne of steel; also bleaching powder, insecticides, paints
Used with iron ore in steel making
Malleable, ductile, good conductor; India has too little of its own
Forms by decomposition of aluminium-rich rocks; gives aluminium, strong yet very light
Odisha (Panchpatmali, Koraput), Amarkantak plateau, Maikal hills, Bilaspur–Katni

visual.alt: Table: manganese, about 10 kilograms per tonne of steel and used in bleaching powder and paints; copper, a good conductor that India lacks, mined at Balaghat, Khetri and Singhbhum; bauxite, the ore of light, strong aluminium, mined in Odisha, Amarkantak and the Maikal hills

slides.narration: Steel needs manganese, about ten kilograms for every tonne. Copper carries electricity in every wire, yet India is seriously short of it, with mines at Balaghat, Khetri and Singhbhum. Bauxite gives us aluminium, which is strong but wonderfully light. Odisha is the leading bauxite state, with its key deposits at Panchpatmali in Koraput.

slides.heading: Mica and limestone
bullets: **Mica**: built of thin layers that peel apart into sheets; it may be clear, black, green, red, yellow or brown.
It **insulates** very well, wastes little power and withstands **high voltage** (high **dielectric strength**), so it is vital for electrical and electronic goods.
Mica areas: **Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh** (Jharkhand), around **Ajmer** (Rajasthan), the **Nellore** belt (Andhra Pradesh).
**Limestone**: in sedimentary rocks of calcium (or calcium and magnesium) carbonates; raw material for **cement**; used to smelt iron ore.

visual.alt: Table: mica is an insulator that splits into thin sheets, used in the electrical and electronic industry; limestone is calcium carbonate rock, used for cement and smelting iron ore

slides.narration: Two non-metallic minerals matter a lot. Mica peels into thin sheets that do not let electricity through, even at high voltage, so it is vital in electrical goods. Its main belt is Koderma, Gaya and Hazaribagh in Jharkhand. Limestone is the basic raw material of cement and is also used when iron ore is smelted in blast furnaces.

slides.heading: Quick check: mica belt
slides.narration: Think of the northern edge of the Chota Nagpur plateau.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: locating iron-ore mines
slides.body_md: Task: *On an outline map of India, locate and label Mayurbhanj, Bailadila and Kudremukh.*
bullets: Step 1 — Mayurbhanj: northern Odisha, bordering Jharkhand and West Bengal (Badampahar mines).
Step 2 — Bailadila: southern Chhattisgarh, in Dantewada (Bastar), near the Telangana border.
Step 3 — Kudremukh: Western Ghats of Karnataka, inland from Mangaluru.
Step 4 — Mark a dot and write the name; add Durg (central Chhattisgarh) and Ballari (eastern Karnataka) the same way.

visual.alt: Table of iron-ore mines with state and landmark: Mayurbhanj in northern Odisha; Durg in central Chhattisgarh near Bhilai; Bailadila in southern Chhattisgarh; Ballari in eastern Karnataka; and Kudremukh in the Western Ghats inland from Mangaluru

slides.narration: Map work is easier with landmarks. Mayurbhanj is in the north of Odisha, touching Jharkhand. Durg is in central Chhattisgarh, close to Bhilai, and Bailadila is in the south, in the Bastar region. In Karnataka, Ballari is in the east, near Andhra Pradesh, and Kudremukh is in the Western Ghats, inland from Mangaluru. One dot, one name, one mark.

slides.heading: Why minerals must be conserved

nodes.label: Workable deposits: a tiny fraction of the crust
Deeper mines, lower-grade ore, higher costs

visual.alt: Flow: workable deposits are a tiny fraction of the crust and formed over millions of years, but are used up in decades, so mines go deeper for lower-grade ore at higher cost, creating the need for conservation

slides.narration: Minerals took millions of years to form, but we can use them up in a few decades. Only a tiny fraction of the Earth's crust holds deposits worth mining. As the best ore is used, mines dig deeper and find poorer ore, so costs rise. That is why minerals are called finite and non-renewable, and why conservation matters.

slides.heading: Quick check: rising costs
slides.body_md: Decide whether the assertion and the reason are true, and whether the reason explains the assertion.
slides.narration: Does the reason explain why the cost goes up?

slides.heading: How to conserve, and the human cost of mining
columns:
**Conserve**

- Plan use in a **sustainable** way.
- Better technology to use **low-grade ores** cheaply.
- **Recycle** metals; use **scrap** and **substitutes**.

**Hazards of mining**

- Dust and fumes cause **lung diseases** in miners.
- Roof collapse, flooding and **fires** in coal mines.
- **Water** contaminated; waste and **slurry** degrade land and pollute rivers.
- Need stricter **safety** and **environmental** laws.

visual.alt: Table: finite reserves call for recycling, substitutes and technology for low-grade ore; lung disease and accidents call for safety rules; polluted water and land call for enforcing environmental laws

slides.narration: Conservation means stretching what we have: recycling metals, using scrap and substitutes, and better technology for low-grade ore. Mining also has a human cost. Miners breathe dust and fumes and risk collapses, floods and fires. Nearby villages find their water polluted and their fields buried under waste. Strict safety and environmental laws are part of using minerals responsibly.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: reading a mining data table
slides.body_md: Data (imagined): *a copper mine produced ore with 2.0 per cent copper in 1980, 1.5 per cent in 2000 and 1.0 per cent in 2020.*
bullets: Step 1 — Read the trend: the copper content halved, from 2.0 to 1.0 per cent.
Step 2 — Calculate: to get 10 tonnes of copper, the mine needed 500 tonnes of ore in 1980 and 1,000 tonnes in 2020.
Step 3 — Interpret: twice as much rock must be dug and processed, so costs and waste rise.
Step 4 — Link to the chapter: minerals are finite; recycle copper and use substitutes.

visual.alt: Line graph of imagined figures: the copper content of ore in an imagined mine falls from 2.0 per cent in 1980 to 1.5 in 2000 and 1.0 in 2020
visual.caption: Imagined figures for practice only.

slides.narration: Here is how to read a mining data question. First describe the trend: the copper in the ore halved. Then calculate what it means. At two per cent, ten tonnes of copper need five hundred tonnes of ore. At one per cent, they need a thousand tonnes. So the mine digs twice as much rock for the same metal. Finish by linking this to conservation.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Natural, uniform, definite structure; ore = concentrated enough to mine
Veins and lodes, beds, residual (bauxite), placers (gold), oceans (salt)
Iron ore (magnetite, hematite; four belts), manganese (10 kg per tonne of steel)
Finite; recycle, substitutes, low-grade ore technology; mining safety

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: minerals and ores, modes of occurrence, ferrous, non-ferrous and non-metallic minerals, and conservation

slides.narration: To sum up. Minerals form in veins, layers, residual deposits, placers and the sea. Iron ore and manganese are the ferrous minerals behind our steel. Copper and bauxite are key non-ferrous metals, and mica and limestone are vital non-metallic ones. Above all, minerals are finite, so we must recycle, find substitutes and mine safely.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Give an **example** with every mode of occurrence: copper (veins), gypsum (evaporation), bauxite (residual), gold (placer), salt (ocean).
Magnetite = **highest iron content**; hematite = **used most**. Do not swap them.
Learn each iron-ore belt with **one mine** and, where given, the **export port**.
Mica answers need its **properties** (insulation, dielectric strength), not just its location.
For conservation, give **measures** (recycling, substitutes, technology), not just reasons.
slides.narration: Some quick tips. Pair every mode of occurrence with an example. Do not mix up magnetite and hematite. Learn each iron belt with a mine and its port. When asked why mica is important, describe its properties. And if a question asks how to conserve minerals, give measures, not just reasons.

decks.title: Minerals and Energy Resources — Part 2: Energy
goals: Describe coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity as conventional sources
Locate the thermal and nuclear power plants on the board map list, and key coalfields and oil fields
Compare nuclear, solar, wind, biogas, tidal and geothermal energy

slides.heading: Minerals and Energy Resources — Part 2
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the fuels that power India today, the cleaner sources that could power it tomorrow, and how to waste less.

visual.alt: Overview of Part 2: conventional sources, coal, petroleum and natural gas, electricity and power plants, non-conventional sources, and conservation
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to Part 2. Every activity needs energy: cooking, farming, factories, trains and the phone in your hand. Most of India's energy still comes from coal, oil and gas, which will not last for ever and pollute the air. We will look at these conventional sources, then at cleaner alternatives, and finally at the cheapest energy of all: energy we do not waste.

slides.heading: Conventional and non-conventional sources

visual.alt: Table: conventional sources are firewood, dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity; non-conventional sources are solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, biogas and nuclear energy

slides.narration: Energy sources are grouped as conventional and non-conventional. Conventional ones have been used for a long time: firewood, dung cake, coal, oil, gas and electricity from dams and thermal plants. Many rural homes still depend on firewood and dung cake, but forests are shrinking, and burning dung wastes precious manure. Non-conventional sources include sun, wind, tides, the Earth's heat, biogas and nuclear power.

slides.heading: How coal forms, and its grades

nodes.label: Bituminous: common commercial coal; metallurgical grade for blast furnaces

visual.alt: Flow of coal formation and grades: plant material in swamps becomes peat, then lignite such as at Neyveli, then bituminous coal including metallurgical grade, and finally anthracite, the highest quality

slides.narration: Coal began as plants in ancient swamps. Buried and squeezed over millions of years, they turned first into peat, which burns poorly, then lignite, a soft brown coal mined at Neyveli. Deeper burial and heat produced bituminous coal, the kind most used in industry, and its best grade, metallurgical coal, smelts iron. Anthracite is the hardest and best of all.

slides.heading: Quick check: grades of coal
slides.body_md: Arrange the forms of coal in order of carbon content.
slides.narration: Start with the swampy, wet stage and end with the hardest coal.

slides.heading: Where India's coal is

rows: Damodar valley (West Bengal–Jharkhand); Godavari, Mahanadi, Son, Wardha valleys
North-east: Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland

visual.alt: Table: Gondwana coal, a little over 200 million years old, is in the Damodar valley with Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro, and in the Godavari, Mahanadi, Son and Wardha valleys; tertiary coal, about 55 million years old, is in the north-east; lignite is at Neyveli

slides.narration: Coal is India's most abundant fossil fuel and supplies much of its electricity. Most of it is Gondwana coal, over two hundred million years old, in the Damodar valley at Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro, and in other river valleys such as the Mahanadi, where Talcher lies. Younger tertiary coal is found in the north-east. Because coal is bulky, power stations and steel plants are often built right beside the fields.

slides.heading: Where petroleum and gas are trapped

nodes.label: Gas at the top of the fold
Oil in porous limestone or sandstone

visual.alt: Layered flow of an oil trap in an anticline, from top to bottom: non-porous cap rock, gas at the top of the fold, oil in porous limestone or sandstone, and non-porous rock below
visual.caption: An anticline trap, from top to bottom (schematic order of layers, not to scale)

slides.narration: Oil and gas move slowly through porous rocks such as sandstone and limestone. In an upfold, called an anticline, they rise to the crest and are trapped there by non-porous rock above. Gas is lighter, so it sits on top of the oil. In India, most oil lies in such traps and in fault traps in young tertiary rocks.

slides.heading: Petroleum and natural gas in India
bullets: Petroleum gives fuel, **lubricants** and raw materials; refineries are a **nodal industry** that feeds makers of synthetic fibres, fertilisers and many chemicals.
Main areas: **Mumbai High** (offshore), **Gujarat** (Ankleshwar the most important; Kalol), **Assam**, the oldest producer (**Digboi**, Naharkatiya, Moran-Hugrijan).
Natural gas: a **cleaner** fuel; large reserves in the **Krishna–Godavari basin**, Mumbai High and the Gulf of Khambhat, and the **Andaman and Nicobar Islands**.
The **HVJ pipeline** links western offshore fields to fertiliser, power and industrial complexes; **CNG** is replacing liquid fuels in vehicles.

visual.alt: Table of oil and gas fields: Mumbai High and Bassein offshore in the Arabian Sea; Ankleshwar and Kalol in Gujarat; Digboi and Naharkatiya in Assam; and the Krishna–Godavari basin on the east coast for gas

slides.narration: Petroleum is India's next big energy source after coal. Its refineries feed many other industries, which is why they are called nodal. Oil comes from Mumbai High in the sea, from Gujarat, and from Assam, India's oldest oil state. Natural gas burns cleaner and is found in the Krishna–Godavari basin and the western offshore fields. Pipelines carry it to power and fertiliser plants.

slides.heading: Quick check: a nodal industry
slides.narration: Think of an industry whose products feed many other industries.

slides.heading: Electricity: thermal, hydel and nuclear

rows: Bhakra Nangal, Damodar Valley Corporation, Kopili
Burning coal, oil or gas turns turbines
Heat from altering atoms of uranium or thorium

visual.alt: Table of electricity types: hydel uses fast-flowing water, is renewable, as at Bhakra Nangal; thermal burns coal, oil or gas, is non-renewable, as at Namrup, Singrauli and Ramagundam; nuclear uses heat from altering atoms of uranium or thorium, as at Narora, Kakrapar, Tarapur and Kalpakkam

slides.narration: Electricity is made by spinning turbines. In hydel plants, falling or fast water does the work, and the water cycle keeps renewing it. In thermal plants, burning coal, oil or gas makes steam, and those fuels will run out. Nuclear plants get heat from changing the structure of atoms of uranium or thorium. The board map list includes three thermal and four nuclear plants.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: locating the power plants
slides.body_md: Task: *On an outline map of India, locate and label the thermal plants Namrup, Singrauli and Ramagundam and the nuclear plants Narora, Kakrapar, Tarapur and Kalpakkam.*
bullets: Step 1 — Thermal: Namrup (Upper Assam), Singrauli (Uttar Pradesh–Madhya Pradesh border), Ramagundam (Telangana, on the Godavari).
Step 2 — Nuclear: Narora (on the Ganga, western Uttar Pradesh), Kakrapar (near Surat, Gujarat).
Step 3 — Nuclear on the coast: Tarapur (north of Mumbai), Kalpakkam (south of Chennai).
Step 4 — Use a small dot and the full name; keep labels outside crowded coastlines.

rows: Coast north of Mumbai; India's first

visual.alt: Table of power plants on the map list with type, state and landmark: Namrup, thermal, Upper Assam; Singrauli, thermal, Uttar Pradesh–Madhya Pradesh coalfield; Ramagundam, thermal, Telangana on the Godavari; Narora, nuclear, Uttar Pradesh on the Ganga; Kakrapar, nuclear, near Surat; Tarapur, nuclear, coast north of Mumbai; Kalpakkam, nuclear, coast south of Chennai

slides.narration: Seven power plants are on the board map list. Group them to remember. Thermal plants sit near fuel: Namrup on Assam's gas, Singrauli on its coalfield, Ramagundam beside the Godavari coal belt. Nuclear plants need lots of cooling water: Narora on the Ganga, Kakrapar near Surat, and Tarapur and Kalpakkam on the coast. Tarapur was India's first nuclear power station.

slides.heading: Electricity mix of an imagined state

x.label: Source (1 = coal, 2 = hydel, 3 = solar, 4 = wind, 5 = nuclear)

visual.alt: Bar chart of imagined figures: coal 55 per cent, hydel 14, solar 17, wind 10 and nuclear 4 per cent of an imagined state's electricity
visual.caption: Imagined figures. Bar 1: coal, 55 per cent. Bar 2: hydel, 14. Bar 3: solar, 17. Bar 4: wind, 10. Bar 5: nuclear, 4.

slides.narration: This imagined state still gets more than half its electricity from coal. Hydel adds fourteen per cent. Solar, wind and nuclear together give thirty-one per cent. Notice how to read such a chart: add the bars you need, and remember that hydel counts as conventional in this chapter, while solar, wind and nuclear are non-conventional.

slides.heading: Why look beyond fossil fuels?

nodes.label: More dependence on coal, oil and gas
Rising prices; worries about secure supply
Turn to renewable and non-conventional sources

visual.alt: Flow: growing energy use increases dependence on coal, oil and gas, leading to rising prices, worries about secure supply, and pollution, so India turns to renewable and non-conventional sources

slides.narration: As India uses more energy, it depends more on coal, oil and gas. Oil and gas prices rise and fall with world events, so supplies can be uncertain, and burning fossil fuels pollutes the air. That is why India is turning to energy from the sun, wind, tides, the Earth's heat, waste and atoms.

slides.heading: Non-conventional sources at a glance

rows: Uranium and thorium: Jharkhand, Aravallis; thorium in Kerala's monazite sands
Photovoltaic cells turn sunlight into electricity
Spreading in rural and remote areas
Nagercoil–Madurai (Tamil Nadu); Jaisalmer; Gujarat, Karnataka, Maharashtra
Decomposing dung and waste make gas
Gulfs of Khambhat and Kachchh; Sundarbans

visual.alt: Table of non-conventional sources: nuclear from uranium and thorium; solar with photovoltaic cells; wind from Nagercoil to Madurai and Jaisalmer; biogas in gobar gas plants; tidal in the Gulfs of Khambhat and Kachchh and the Sundarbans; geothermal in the Parvati and Puga valleys

slides.narration: Here are the six non-conventional sources. Nuclear power uses uranium and thorium. Solar panels turn sunlight straight into electricity. Wind farms line the gap near Nagercoil. Gobar gas plants turn dung into fuel and better manure. Tides can be trapped in the Gulfs of Khambhat and Kachchh. And hot springs in the Parvati and Puga valleys show the Earth's own heat.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: planning a 5-mark comparison
slides.body_md: Question: *Compare conventional and non-conventional sources of energy.* (about 120 words)
bullets: Step 1 — Choose five headings: examples, renewability, pollution, cost and scale, availability in India.
Step 2 — For each heading, write both sides in one sentence.
Step 3 — Add Indian examples: coal at Jharia, wind near Nagercoil.
Step 4 — End with one line on why India needs both for now.

rows: Falling costs; often small or local

visual.alt: Table comparing conventional and non-conventional energy on five headings: examples, renewability, pollution, cost and scale, and steadiness of supply

slides.narration: Comparison questions reward structure. Pick five headings and write both sides under each, so the examiner can tick five clear points. Add Indian examples to show real knowledge. A final line, saying that India still needs both while it shifts to cleaner sources, shows balanced thinking and rounds the answer off well.

slides.heading: Conserving energy
columns:
**Why**

- Every sector needs energy, but fossil fuels are **finite**.
- **Conservation** and more **renewable energy** are the **twin planks** of sustainable energy.
- **Energy saved is energy produced.**

**How**

- Use **public transport** instead of private vehicles.
- **Switch off** lights and appliances not in use.
- Use **power-saving devices**.
- Use **non-conventional** sources where possible.

visual.alt: Flow: use less through public transport and switching off, use better with power-saving devices, and use cleaner renewable sources, leading to sustainable energy

slides.narration: The cheapest unit of energy is the one you never use. Energy saved is energy produced. India's path to sustainable energy rests on two planks: conserving energy and using more renewable sources. You can help every day: take the bus or cycle, switch off lights and fans, choose efficient appliances, and use solar heaters where you can.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: Peat → lignite → bituminous → anthracite; Gondwana (Damodar valley) and tertiary (north-east); Neyveli lignite
Anticlines and fault traps; Mumbai High, Gujarat, Assam; gas in Krishna–Godavari; HVJ pipeline
Thermal: Namrup, Singrauli, Ramagundam. Nuclear: Narora, Kakrapar, Tarapur, Kalpakkam
Nuclear, solar, wind, biogas, tidal, geothermal
Use less, use better, use cleaner

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: coal, oil and gas, electricity, the power plant map list, non-conventional sources, and conservation

slides.narration: To sum up. Coal is India's most abundant fossil fuel, found mainly in the Damodar valley. Oil and gas come from Mumbai High, Gujarat and Assam, with gas in the Krishna–Godavari basin. Electricity comes from water, fossil fuels and atoms. Learn the seven power plants for the map. And remember the future: renewable sources plus conservation.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: Hydel is **conventional** but **renewable**; nuclear is **non-conventional** but its fuel is **limited**.
Assam is the **oldest** oil-producing state; Ankleshwar is Gujarat's **most important** field.
Map: thermal = **Namrup, Singrauli, Ramagundam**; nuclear = **Narora, Kakrapar, Tarapur, Kalpakkam**.
Biogas: always mention the **twin benefits** (fuel and manure).
Conservation answers need **actions**, not slogans.
slides.narration: Final tips. Watch the classification traps: hydel is conventional yet renewable. Know Assam as the oldest oil state. Practise the seven power plants until you can place them without looking. For biogas, always give both benefits. And when asked how to save energy, write real actions you could take.

sections.heading: 1. Minerals and how they occur
sections.body_md:
A **mineral** is a naturally formed substance with a uniform make-up and a definite internal structure. **Rocks** are combinations of minerals; a few, such as **limestone**, consist of one. An **ore** is a mineral mixed with other elements and concentrated enough for mining to be worthwhile.

**Modes of occurrence**
1. **Veins and lodes** in cracks, faults and joints of **igneous and metamorphic** rocks, where hot fluids and gases rising through the rock harden as they cool (small = veins, large = lodes). Tin, copper, zinc, lead.
2. **Beds or layers** in **sedimentary** rocks, formed by deposition and concentration over long periods under heat and pressure (coal, some iron ore); **evaporation** in dry regions leaves gypsum, potash salt and sodium salt.
3. **Residual deposits:** weathering removes soluble parts and leaves the ore, e.g. **bauxite**.
4. **Placer deposits:** alluvial sands of valley floors and hill bases hold minerals that water does not dissolve or wear away — **gold, silver, tin, platinum**.
5. **Ocean waters and beds:** **common salt, magnesium, bromine**; **manganese nodules** on the sea floor.

**Distribution:** the old rocks of the **peninsula** hold most coal, metallic minerals and mica; sedimentary rocks in **Gujarat and Assam** hold most petroleum; **Rajasthan** has many non-ferrous minerals; the **northern plains** have almost none. **Rat-hole mining** of coal by families in Meghalaya (e.g. Jowai, Cherrapunjee) has been declared illegal by the **National Green Tribunal**.

key_terms.definition_md: A naturally formed substance with a uniform make-up and a definite internal structure.
A deposit in which a mineral is concentrated enough to be mined profitably.
Water-resistant minerals such as gold collected in the sands of valley floors and hill bases.

sections.heading: 2. Ferrous, non-ferrous and non-metallic minerals
sections.body_md:
**Classification:** metallic — **ferrous** (iron ore, manganese, nickel, cobalt), **non-ferrous** (copper, lead, tin, bauxite), **precious** (gold, silver, platinum); **non-metallic** (mica, salt, potash, sulphur, granite, limestone, marble, sandstone); **energy** minerals (coal, petroleum, natural gas). Ferrous minerals make up about three-quarters of the value of metallic minerals produced.

**Iron ore** — the basic mineral of industry. **Magnetite**: the finest ore, up to about **70 per cent** iron, strongly magnetic, valued in the electrical industry. **Hematite**: **50–60 per cent** iron, the ore used in the **largest quantity**.
- **Odisha–Jharkhand belt:** high-grade hematite at **Badampahar** (Mayurbhanj and Kendujhar, Odisha); **Gua and Noamundi** (Singhbhum, Jharkhand).
- **Durg–Bastar–Chandrapur belt** (Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra): very high-grade hematite of the **Bailadila** hills (14 deposits), well suited to steel making; exported to Japan and South Korea via **Visakhapatnam**.
- **Ballari–Chitradurga–Chikkamagaluru–Tumakuru belt** (Karnataka): large reserves; **Kudremukh** in the Western Ghats was developed as a 100 per cent export unit, its ore sent as **slurry** by pipeline to a port near **Mangaluru**.
- **Maharashtra–Goa belt:** Goa and **Ratnagiri**; ore of lower quality but mined efficiently and exported via **Marmagao**.

**Manganese:** about **10 kg** per tonne of steel (ferro-manganese alloy); also bleaching powder, insecticides, paints.

**Copper:** India has too little of its own. Malleable, ductile, a good conductor: cables, electronics, chemicals. **Balaghat** (Madhya Pradesh), **Khetri** (Rajasthan), **Singhbhum** (Jharkhand).

**Bauxite:** an earthy ore formed by the decomposition of rocks rich in **aluminium silicates**; gives **aluminium**, which is strong yet very light, conducts well and is easily shaped. **Amarkantak plateau, Maikal hills, Bilaspur–Katni** plateau; **Odisha** leads, with **Panchpatmali** (Koraput) its key deposit.

**Mica:** thin layers that peel apart into sheets; a very good **insulator** with high **dielectric strength** that withstands high voltage — vital in electrical and electronic industries. **Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh** (Jharkhand), around **Ajmer** (Rajasthan), **Nellore** belt (Andhra Pradesh).

**Limestone:** rocks of calcium or calcium–magnesium carbonates in sedimentary formations; basic raw material of **cement**; used to **smelt iron ore**.

**Mines on the map list (locate):** iron ore — Mayurbhanj, Durg, Bailadila, Ballari, Kudremukh.

key_terms.definition_md: Minerals containing iron, such as iron ore, manganese, nickel and cobalt.
The richest iron ore, with up to about 70 per cent iron and strong magnetic properties.
An iron ore with 50–60 per cent iron, used by industry in the largest quantity.

sections.heading: 3. Conservation of minerals
sections.body_md:
- Industry and agriculture depend heavily on minerals, yet workable deposits are a **tiny fraction** of the Earth's crust.
- Minerals form over **millions of years** but are consumed rapidly; replenishment is negligible on a human timescale, so they are **finite and non-renewable**.
- Continued extraction means ore must come from **greater depths** and is of **lower quality**, so **costs rise**.
- **Measures:** plan use sustainably; improve **technology** to use **low-grade ores** at low cost; **recycle** metals; use **scrap** and **substitutes**.
- **Hazards of mining:** dust and harmful fumes cause **pulmonary (lung) diseases**; risk of **roof collapse, inundation and fires** in coal mines; **water** sources contaminated; dumping of **waste and slurry** degrades land and soil and pollutes streams and rivers. Stricter **safety regulations** and **environmental laws** are essential.

key_terms.definition_md: A resource that forms so slowly that, once used, it cannot be replaced on a human timescale.
Recovering metals from scrap so that they can be used again.
A watery mixture of fine waste or ore produced by mining and processing.

sections.heading: 4. Conventional sources of energy
sections.body_md:
**Conventional:** firewood, cattle dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas, electricity (hydel and thermal). Firewood and dung cake are common in rural homes, but forests are shrinking and burning dung wastes **manure**.

**Coal** — India's most abundant fossil fuel; used for power, industry and homes. Formed from plant material compressed over millions of years: **peat** (low carbon, high moisture) → **lignite** (low-grade brown coal, soft, moist; main reserves at **Neyveli**, Tamil Nadu, used for power) → **bituminous** (most common commercial coal; high-grade **metallurgical** coal for blast furnaces) → **anthracite** (highest quality). **Gondwana** coal (a little over 200 million years): **Damodar valley** — **Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro**; also the Godavari, Mahanadi (**Talcher**), Son and Wardha valleys. **Tertiary** coal (about 55 million years): Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland. Coal is **heavy**, and much of its weight is left as ash, so heavy industries and thermal plants are built **on or near coalfields**.

**Petroleum** — fuel, **lubricants** and raw materials; refineries are a **nodal industry** that feeds makers of synthetic fibres, fertilisers and many chemicals. Found in **anticlines** and **fault traps** in tertiary rocks: oil in **porous** limestone or sandstone, sealed by **non-porous** layers; gas above oil. Areas: **Mumbai High** (offshore), **Gujarat** (**Ankleshwar** most important; Kalol), **Assam** — the oldest producer (**Digboi**, Naharkatiya, Moran-Hugrijan).

**Natural gas** — a cleaner fuel (less carbon dioxide); energy source and petrochemical raw material. Reserves: **Krishna–Godavari basin**, Mumbai High and allied fields, Gulf of Khambhat, **Andaman and Nicobar Islands**. The **Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur (HVJ)** pipeline links Mumbai High and Bassein with fertiliser, power and industrial complexes; **CNG** is replacing liquid fuels in vehicles.

**Electricity** — **hydel** (fast-flowing water, renewable; Bhakra Nangal, Damodar Valley Corporation, Kopili) and **thermal** (coal, petroleum, natural gas; non-renewable).

**Board map list (locate and label):** thermal — **Namrup** (Assam), **Singrauli** (Uttar Pradesh–Madhya Pradesh), **Ramagundam** (Telangana); nuclear — **Narora** (Uttar Pradesh), **Kakrapar** (Gujarat), **Tarapur** (Maharashtra), **Kalpakkam** (Tamil Nadu). Coal mines (Raniganj, Bokaro, Talcher, Neyveli) and oil fields (Digboi, Naharkatiya, Mumbai High, Bassein, Kalol, Ankleshwar) are also on the syllabus map list.

key_terms.definition_md: An industry whose products are raw materials for many other industries, such as petroleum refining.
An upfold in rock layers, at whose crest oil and gas can be trapped.
High-grade bituminous coal used to smelt iron in blast furnaces.

sections.heading: 5. Non-conventional sources and conservation of energy
sections.body_md:
Growing energy use has increased dependence on **fossil fuels**; rising oil and gas prices and possible shortages raise doubts about **energy security**, and fossil fuels cause serious **pollution**. Hence the need for **renewable** sources.
- **Nuclear (atomic) energy:** heat released by altering the structure of atoms generates electricity. **Uranium and thorium** occur in **Jharkhand** and the **Aravallis** of Rajasthan; **monazite sands** of Kerala are rich in thorium.
- **Solar energy:** **photovoltaic** technology turns sunlight directly into electricity; spreading in rural and remote areas; large plants reduce dependence on firewood and dung cake, saving forests and manure.
- **Wind power:** the largest cluster runs from **Nagercoil to Madurai** (Tamil Nadu); also Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Gujarat, Kerala, Maharashtra, Lakshadweep; **Nagercoil and Jaisalmer** are known for effective use.
- **Biogas:** shrubs, farm waste and animal and human waste decompose to give gas with higher thermal efficiency than kerosene, dung cake and charcoal. **Gobar gas plants** give **twin benefits** — fuel and better **manure** — and save trees.
- **Tidal energy:** **floodgate dams** across inlets trap water at high tide and release it through turbines; **Gulf of Khambhat, Gulf of Kachchh** and the **Sundarbans** delta are ideal.
- **Geothermal energy:** where the Earth is hot at shallow depth, groundwater turns to **steam** that drives turbines; hundreds of hot springs; experimental projects in the **Parvati valley** near **Manikaran** (Himachal Pradesh) and the **Puga valley** (Ladakh).

**Conservation of energy:** energy is needed by every sector; **energy conservation** and **more renewable energy** are the **twin planks** of sustainable energy. Use **public transport**, switch off unused electricity, use **power-saving devices**, use non-conventional sources. **Energy saved is energy produced.**

key_terms.definition_md: Technology that converts sunlight directly into electricity.
Gas produced by decomposing organic matter such as dung and farm waste, used as fuel.
Energy from the Earth's internal heat, often tapped as steam from hot groundwater.

rows: Gulfs of Khambhat and Kachchh, Sundarbans

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Swapping **magnetite** (richest) and **hematite** (most used).
- Calling **hydel** non-renewable or **thermal** renewable.
- Placing **tertiary** coal in the Damodar valley (it is in the north-east; the Damodar valley has **Gondwana** coal).
- Saying placer minerals dissolve in water: they **resist** corrosion.
- Forgetting the **twin benefits** of biogas (fuel and manure).

**How marks are awarded**
- 1-mark map items: correct place, clear dot, correct name (power plants on the board list; mines and oil fields on the syllabus list).
- 2- and 3-mark answers: one distinct point per mark, each with a place or example.
- 5-mark answers: five distinct points; comparison answers cover both sides under each heading; evaluation answers end with a judgement.
- Case-based (4): two short parts from the data or passage and a 2-mark part from your own knowledge.

questions.stem_md: Which description fits a mineral best?

options.text_md: Any rock found on the Earth's surface
A naturally formed substance with a uniform make-up and a definite internal structure
A substance made in a factory from several metals
Any fuel that can be burnt

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Geologists describe a mineral as a natural substance with uniform composition and an ordered internal structure.
Step 2: Rocks are combinations of minerals, so (a) is too broad; (c) is an alloy; (d) mixes up minerals with fuels. So (b).

questions.stem_md: An "ore" is

options.text_md: an accumulation of a mineral mixed with other elements, rich enough to make extraction pay
a mineral found only in ocean water
any rock that contains no metal
a type of coal

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Minerals are usually found mixed with other elements.
Step 2: When the mineral is concentrated enough for extraction to be commercially worthwhile, the deposit is called an ore. So (a).

questions.stem_md: In igneous and metamorphic rocks, small occurrences of minerals in cracks and joints are called veins. What are the larger occurrences called?

options.text_md: Lodes
Placers
Strata
Nodules

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Molten and gaseous material forced up through cracks cools into mineral deposits.
Step 2: Smaller ones are veins and larger ones are lodes, so (a). Tin, copper, zinc and lead are obtained from them.

questions.stem_md: Bauxite forms when surface rocks decompose and the soluble parts are washed away. What does this leave behind?

options.text_md: Veins of molten metal
A leftover layer of weathered rock that is rich in the ore
Layers of evaporated salt
Nodules on the ocean floor

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Weathering removes the soluble constituents of the rock.
Step 2: What is left behind is weathered rock rich in the ore, which is how bauxite forms. So (b).

questions.stem_md: An imagined prospector pans the sand of a stream bed at the foot of hills and finds grains of gold. What kind of deposit is this?

options.text_md: A lode
An evaporite bed
A placer deposit
A manganese nodule

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Minerals that resist corrosion by water collect in the sands of valley floors and hill bases.
Step 2: These alluvial deposits are placers; gold, silver, tin and platinum occur in them. So (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is obtained largely from ocean water?

options.text_md: Mica
Coal
Iron ore
Common salt

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Most minerals in sea water are too thinly spread to be useful.
Step 2: Common salt, magnesium and bromine are largely obtained from it, so (d). The ocean bed also has manganese nodules.

questions.stem_md: Why are the vast alluvial plains of north India almost without economic minerals?

options.text_md: They are made of young river sediments, not the old rocks in which most minerals occur
They receive too much rain
Mining is banned in the plains
All their minerals have already been used up

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Most of India's coal, metallic minerals and mica are in the old rocks of the peninsula.
Step 2: The northern plains are built of recent alluvium, so they hold almost no economic minerals: (a).

questions.stem_md: In parts of Meghalaya, such as around Jowai and Cherrapunjee, family members dug coal through long, narrow tunnels. What is this practice called, and how has it been treated?

options.text_md: Open-cast mining; it is the main method of large companies
Placer mining; it is encouraged by the state
Offshore drilling; it is used only for oil
Rat-hole mining; the National Green Tribunal has declared such mining illegal

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Long narrow tunnels dug by families are known as rat-hole mining.
Step 2: Because of its dangers to workers and the environment, the National Green Tribunal declared it illegal. So (d).

questions.stem_md: Which group lists only non-ferrous metallic minerals?

options.text_md: Iron ore, manganese, nickel
Mica, limestone, granite
Copper, lead, tin, bauxite
Coal, petroleum, natural gas

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Ferrous minerals contain iron (iron ore, manganese, nickel, cobalt); non-metallic include mica and limestone; energy minerals are coal, petroleum and gas.
Step 2: Copper, lead, tin and bauxite are non-ferrous metals, so (c).

questions.stem_md: Which iron ore has the highest iron content (up to about 70 per cent) and is strongly magnetic?

options.text_md: Hematite
Limonite
Bauxite
Magnetite

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Magnetite is the richest iron ore, with up to about 70 per cent iron, and is valued in the electrical industry.
Step 2: Hematite has 50–60 per cent iron but is used in greater quantity. So (d).

questions.stem_md: Hematite has a lower iron content than magnetite. Why is it still called the most important industrial iron ore?

options.text_md: It contains no iron at all
It is the only ore found in India
It is the ore used in the largest quantity by industry
It is used only for making aluminium

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Hematite contains about 50–60 per cent iron.
Step 2: It is the ore that industry uses in by far the greatest quantity, which makes it the most important industrially. So (c).

questions.stem_md: The Bailadila range of hills, with very high-grade hematite well suited to steel making, lies in

options.text_md: the Bastar district of Chhattisgarh
the Ratnagiri district of Maharashtra
the Koraput district of Odisha
the Western Ghats of Karnataka

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Bailadila is part of the Durg–Bastar–Chandrapur belt.
Step 2: It lies in Bastar (now Dantewada) district of Chhattisgarh, so (a). Its ore has been exported to Japan and South Korea through Visakhapatnam port.

questions.stem_md: Kudremukh in the Western Ghats of Karnataka is known in the history of Indian iron mining because

options.text_md: it was the first coalfield in India
it is India's main source of mica
it was developed as a 100 per cent export unit, sending its ore as slurry through a pipeline to a port near Mangaluru
it supplies bauxite to aluminium smelters

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Kudremukh's large iron deposits were mined for export.
Step 2: The ore was moved as slurry through a pipeline to a port near Mangaluru, so (c).

questions.stem_md: Which mine is correctly matched with its iron-ore belt?

options.text_md: Gua and Noamundi — Maharashtra–Goa belt
Badampahar — Odisha–Jharkhand belt
Bailadila — Ballari–Chitradurga–Chikkamagaluru–Tumakuru belt
Kudremukh — Durg–Bastar–Chandrapur belt

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Badampahar (Mayurbhanj and Kendujhar, Odisha) and Gua and Noamundi (Singhbhum, Jharkhand) are in the Odisha–Jharkhand belt.
Step 2: Bailadila is in the Durg–Bastar–Chandrapur belt and Kudremukh in the Karnataka belt. So (b).

questions.stem_md: Roughly how much manganese is needed to make one tonne of steel, and what else is it used for?

options.text_md: About 10 kg; also bleaching powder, insecticides and paints
About 1 tonne; also electric cables
About 100 kg; also aircraft bodies
None; it is used only for fertilisers

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Steel making needs about 10 kg of manganese per tonne, mainly via ferro-manganese alloy.
Step 2: Manganese is also used in bleaching powder, insecticides and paints. So (a).

questions.stem_md: Copper is widely used in electrical cables and electronics. Which properties explain this?

options.text_md: It is brittle and a poor conductor
It is malleable, ductile and a good conductor of electricity
It is radioactive
It splits into thin transparent sheets

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Copper can be beaten into shape (malleable) and drawn into wires (ductile).
Step 2: It conducts electricity well, so (b). (d) describes mica.

questions.stem_md: Which of these are leading copper-producing areas of India?

options.text_md: Digboi, Ankaleshwar and Kalol
Neyveli, Jharia and Raniganj
Balaghat (Madhya Pradesh), Khetri (Rajasthan) and Singhbhum (Jharkhand)
Koderma, Gaya and Hazaribagh

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Balaghat, Khetri and Singhbhum are the leading copper areas; India is short of copper overall.
Step 2: (b) are coalfields, (a) oilfields, (d) the mica belt. So (c).

questions.stem_md: Aluminium, made from bauxite, is an important metal mainly because it

options.text_md: is heavier than iron
is a fuel
is strong yet very light, conducts electricity well and is easy to shape
cannot be shaped

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Aluminium is strong like some metals yet very light.
Step 2: It also conducts well and can be shaped easily, so (c).

questions.stem_md: Panchpatmali in Koraput district is the most important bauxite deposit of

options.text_md: Kerala
Jharkhand
Gujarat
Odisha

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Odisha is the largest bauxite-producing state.
Step 2: Its most important deposits are at Panchpatmali in Koraput district, so (d). Other bauxite areas are the Amarkantak plateau, Maikal hills and the Bilaspur–Katni plateau.

questions.stem_md: Why is mica so important in the electrical and electronics industries?

options.text_md: It is a good conductor of heat
It is magnetic
It is a fuel
It insulates very well, wastes little power and does not break down under high voltage

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Electrical devices need materials that insulate and do not break down under high voltage.
Step 2: Mica peels into thin sheets that insulate well and withstand high voltage, so (d).

questions.stem_md: Which belt is the leading producer of mica in India?

options.text_md: Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh belt of Jharkhand
Ballari–Chitradurga belt of Karnataka
Durg–Bastar belt of Chhattisgarh
Maharashtra–Goa belt

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Mica deposits occur on the northern edge of the Chota Nagpur plateau.
Step 2: The Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh belt of Jharkhand leads; Ajmer (Rajasthan) and the Nellore belt (Andhra Pradesh) are also important. So (a).

questions.stem_md: An imagined company wants to build a cement plant. Which mineral should it locate close to, and why?

options.text_md: Mica, because it insulates electricity
Limestone, because it is the basic raw material of cement
Copper, because it conducts electricity
Gold, because it is precious

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Cement is made mainly from limestone, which is bulky.
Step 2: Locating near limestone cuts transport costs, so (b). Limestone is also needed for smelting iron ore in blast furnaces.

questions.stem_md: Why must minerals be conserved?

options.text_md: They form very slowly over geological time, so they are finite and non-renewable
They are renewed every year by rain
They are found everywhere in large amounts
They have no use in industry

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Workable mineral deposits are a tiny fraction of the Earth's crust.
Step 2: They are used up far faster than geological processes can form them, so they are finite and non-renewable: (a).

questions.stem_md: An imagined mine has worked the same iron deposit for sixty years. What is most likely to happen to its costs and ore over time?

options.text_md: Costs fall because the ore gets richer with depth
Costs stay the same for ever
The mine starts producing coal instead
Costs rise because ore must be dug from greater depths and its quality falls

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: As the easily reached ore is used, mining goes deeper.
Step 2: Deeper ore costs more to extract and is often of lower grade, so (d).

questions.stem_md: Which practice helps conserve mineral resources most directly?

options.text_md: Exporting all high-grade ore
Recycling metals and using scrap and substitutes
Opening more mines in forests
Burning coal more quickly

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Conservation means getting more use from minerals already extracted.
Step 2: Recycling metals and using scrap and substitutes reduce the need for new ore, so (b). Better technology to use low-grade ore also helps.

questions.stem_md: Workers in an imagined underground coal mine breathe dust and fumes for years. Which health risk does this create most directly?

options.text_md: Night blindness
Malaria
Pulmonary (lung) diseases
Broken bones

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Dust and harmful fumes are inhaled.
Step 2: They damage the lungs, making miners vulnerable to pulmonary diseases, so (c). Mines also face roof collapse, flooding and fires.

questions.stem_md: Which group consists only of conventional sources of energy?

options.text_md: Solar, wind, tidal
Firewood, cattle dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity
Biogas, geothermal, solar
Tidal, nuclear, wind

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Conventional sources are those long in use: firewood, dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity (hydel and thermal).
Step 2: Solar, wind, tidal, geothermal, biogas and atomic energy are non-conventional. So (b).

questions.stem_md: Why is burning cattle dung cake as fuel discouraged?

options.text_md: It produces nuclear waste
It is too costly
It uses up valuable manure that could enrich fields
It is illegal everywhere

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Dung is an excellent natural manure.
Step 2: Burning it as fuel wastes that manure, and firewood is getting scarce as forests shrink. So (c).

questions.stem_md: Which coal is a low-grade brown coal, soft, with high moisture, mined mainly at Neyveli?

options.text_md: Anthracite
Bituminous
Peat
Lignite

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Lignite is low-grade brown coal, soft and moist.
Step 2: India's main lignite reserves are at Neyveli in Tamil Nadu, used to generate electricity. So (d).
Step 3: Peat has even less carbon; bituminous is the common commercial coal; anthracite is the highest quality.

questions.stem_md: The major resources of Gondwana coal, a little over 200 million years old, are found in

options.text_md: the north-eastern states
the Thar desert
the Damodar valley of West Bengal and Jharkhand
the Kashmir valley

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Gondwana coal, mostly metallurgical, lies in the Damodar valley: Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro.
Step 2: The Godavari, Mahanadi, Son and Wardha valleys also have coal. So (c).
Step 3: Tertiary coal (about 55 million years old) is in the north-east, so (a) is wrong.

questions.stem_md: Why are heavy industries and thermal power stations often built on or near coalfields?

options.text_md: Coal is light and easy to transport over long distances
Coalfields have the best ports
Coal can be used only where it is mined
Coal is heavy, and much of its weight is left behind as ash after burning, so hauling it far is costly

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Coal is heavy and much of its weight is lost as ash after burning.
Step 2: It is cheaper to bring the plant to the coal than the coal to the plant, so (d).

questions.stem_md: In folded rocks, where is petroleum usually trapped?

options.text_md: In the crest of an upfold (anticline), in porous rock sealed by non-porous layers
In the bottom of a downfold, in granite
Only in river sand
In ice sheets

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Oil moves through porous limestone or sandstone and rises.
Step 2: In an anticline it collects at the crest, held in by non-porous layers above and below; gas, being lighter, sits above the oil. So (a). Oil is also found in fault traps.

questions.stem_md: Petroleum refineries are called a "nodal industry" because they

options.text_md: use only coal
are always built at river junctions
supply raw materials to many other industries, such as those making synthetic fibres, fertilisers and chemicals
produce electricity only

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A node is a point from which many links spread out.
Step 2: Refinery products feed synthetic textile, fertiliser and many chemical industries, so (c).

questions.stem_md: Which state is the oldest oil-producing state of India, with fields at Digboi, Naharkatiya and Moran-Hugrijan?

options.text_md: Gujarat
Maharashtra
Rajasthan
Assam

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Oil was first produced in India in Assam.
Step 2: Digboi, Naharkatiya and Moran-Hugrijan are its main fields, so (d). Ankleshwar is the most important field of Gujarat.

questions.stem_md: Natural gas is considered an environment-friendly fuel mainly because

options.text_md: it is found only in deserts
it emits less carbon dioxide when burnt than coal or oil
it is renewable
it produces no heat

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Burning gas releases less carbon dioxide than burning coal or oil for the same energy.
Step 2: So it is seen as a cleaner fuel, (b). It is still a fossil fuel, so (c) is wrong.

questions.stem_md: Where have large reserves of natural gas been discovered on India's east coast?

options.text_md: The Krishna–Godavari basin
The Gulf of Kachchh
The Thar desert
The Damodar valley

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The Krishna–Godavari basin off the east coast holds large gas reserves.
Step 2: On the west coast, Mumbai High and allied fields, with finds in the Gulf of Khambhat, are important; the Andaman and Nicobar Islands also have reserves. So (a).

questions.stem_md: What is the key difference between hydel and thermal electricity?

options.text_md: Hydel burns coal; thermal uses running water
Hydel uses fast-flowing water, a renewable resource; thermal burns coal, petroleum or gas, which are non-renewable
Both use only nuclear fuel
Thermal power is renewable; hydel is not

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Hydroelectric plants spin turbines with falling or fast-flowing water, which the water cycle renews.
Step 2: Thermal plants burn fossil fuels, which are non-renewable. So (b).

questions.stem_md: Uranium and thorium for nuclear power are found in Jharkhand and the Aravalli ranges of Rajasthan. Which other source is rich in thorium?

options.text_md: Monazite sands of Kerala
Coal of Jharia
Salt of the Rann of Kachchh
Bauxite of Koraput

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Monazite sands along the Kerala coast are rich in thorium.
Step 2: So (a).

questions.stem_md: Photovoltaic technology

options.text_md: uses tides to drive turbines
burns cattle dung to make gas
uses heat from the Earth's interior
converts sunlight directly into electricity

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Photovoltaic cells (solar panels) turn light directly into electric current.
Step 2: So (d).

questions.stem_md: An imagined remote village burns firewood and dung cakes for cooking and lighting. A solar power plant is installed. Which two benefits does the chapter link to such a change?

options.text_md: More coal mining and more manure burnt
Higher demand for kerosene and more deforestation
Less pressure on forests and more dung available as manure for farming
More pollution and more firewood use

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Solar power reduces the need to burn firewood and dung.
Step 2: Forests are spared, and dung can go to the fields as manure, so (c).

questions.stem_md: The largest cluster of wind farms in India stretches from Nagercoil to Madurai in

options.text_md: Rajasthan
Gujarat
Kerala
Tamil Nadu

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Strong, steady winds blow through the gap at the southern tip of the Western Ghats.
Step 2: The largest wind-farm cluster runs from Nagercoil to Madurai in Tamil Nadu, so (d). Jaisalmer is also known for wind energy.

questions.stem_md: Gobar gas plants give "twin benefits" to rural households. What are they?

options.text_md: Coal and oil
Energy for cooking and lighting, and better-quality manure
Uranium and thorium
Electricity and steel

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Cattle dung decomposes in the plant to give gas for fuel.
Step 2: The leftover slurry is a richer manure than dung cake ash, so (b). It also saves trees and manure from being burnt.

questions.stem_md: Which areas of India offer ideal conditions for tidal energy?

options.text_md: The Thar desert and the Aravallis
The Gulf of Khambhat, the Gulf of Kachchh and the Gangetic delta in the Sundarbans
The Nilgiris and the Western Ghats
The Kashmir valley

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Tidal power needs inlets with a large tidal range where floodgates can trap water.
Step 2: The Gulfs of Khambhat and Kachchh and the Sundarbans delta suit this, so (b).

questions.stem_md: In an imagined valley, groundwater comes out of the ground as steam. Why could this valley be suitable for a geothermal power plant?

options.text_md: Its rocks are hot at shallow depth, so groundwater turns to steam that can drive turbines
It has strong winds all year
It has a large tidal range
It has large coal reserves

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Where the geothermal gradient is high, rocks near the surface are very hot.
Step 2: Groundwater absorbs this heat and rises as steam, which can spin turbines. So (a).

questions.stem_md: Which pair of measures does the chapter treat as the "twin planks" of sustainable energy?

options.text_md: More coal mining and more oil imports
Burning more firewood and dung cake
Building more thermal plants and more highways
Energy conservation and greater use of renewable energy sources

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Sustainable energy needs us to use less and to use cleaner sources.
Step 2: So promoting conservation and renewable energy are the twin planks: (d).

questions.stem_md: An imagined city wants to cut its fuel use and pollution quickly. Which measure would help most?

options.text_md: Building more parking for private cars
Subsidising diesel generators
Better public transport, with power-saving appliances in homes and offices
Leaving street lights on during the day

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Transport and electricity use are major consumers of fuel.
Step 2: Public transport and power-saving devices reduce both fuel use and pollution, so (c).

questions.stem_md:

questions.solution_md:

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Gold and platinum are found in placer deposits.

**Reason (R):** Placer minerals are those that dissolve easily in water.

questions.solution_md:

questions.stem_md:

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** India has too little copper of its own, in both reserves and production.

**Reason (R):** Copper is a poor conductor of electricity.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution_md:

questions.stem_md:

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.stem_md: What is an ore? Why does the concentration of the mineral in it matter?

answer.model_answer_md: An **ore** is a natural accumulation of a mineral mixed with **other elements**. The mineral must be **concentrated** enough for extraction to be **commercially worthwhile**; a thin scatter costs more to mine than it earns.

questions.solution_md: Definition and the economic condition.

questions.stem_md: How are veins and lodes formed? Name two metals obtained from them.

answer.model_answer_md: Molten and gaseous material is forced up through **cracks, faults and joints** in igneous and metamorphic rocks and **cools and solidifies** there; small deposits are veins, large ones **lodes**. **Tin** and **copper** (also zinc, lead) come from them.

questions.solution_md: Formation plus two metals.

marking_scheme.step: Formation in cracks as material cools

questions.stem_md: What are placer deposits? Give two examples of minerals found in them.

answer.model_answer_md: Placers are **alluvial deposits** in the sands of **valley floors** and the base of hills, holding minerals that **water does not corrode**. Examples: **gold** and **platinum** (also silver, tin).

questions.solution_md: Definition and two examples.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between magnetite and hematite.

answer.model_answer_md: **Magnetite** is the richest iron ore, with up to about **70 per cent** iron, and is strongly **magnetic**. **Hematite** has less iron (**50–60 per cent**) but is the ore industry uses in the **largest quantity**.

questions.solution_md: Contrast iron content and use.

questions.stem_md: Why is mica important for the electrical industry? Name one area where it is mined.

answer.model_answer_md: Mica peels into **thin sheets** that **insulate** very well, waste little power and withstand **high voltage**. It is mined in the **Koderma–Gaya–Hazaribagh** belt of Jharkhand.

questions.solution_md: Properties plus an area.

questions.stem_md: Give two uses of limestone and state where it is usually found.

answer.model_answer_md: Limestone is the **basic raw material** of the **cement** industry and is needed for **smelting iron ore** in blast furnaces. It occurs in **sedimentary rocks** made of calcium (or calcium and magnesium) carbonates.

questions.solution_md: Two uses and its occurrence.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why minerals need to be conserved.

questions.stem_md: A geologist finds an imagined mineral that peels into thin, see-through sheets, does not let electricity pass even at high voltage, and loses very little power. Which industry would value it most?

options.text_md: Cement
Electrical and electronics
Fertiliser
Sugar

questions.solution_md:

Step 2: These make it essential in electrical and electronic goods, so (b).

questions.stem_md: An imagined state exports most of its high-grade iron ore as raw ore. Which argument best supports limiting such exports?

options.text_md: Iron ore is finite, and processing it at home into steel would conserve reserves for future industry and add more value
Iron ore is renewable, so exports do not matter
Exporting ore creates no income at all
Iron ore cannot be used to make steel in India

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: High-grade ore is a non-renewable resource.
Step 2: Using it for domestic steel conserves it for the country's own industry and earns more than selling raw ore, so (a).
Step 3: (b), (c) and (d) are false.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined copper deposits are offered for mining. Deposit P: 2 per cent copper, 50 metres deep, next to a railway. Deposit Q: 0.5 per cent copper, 400 metres deep, far from any road. Which is a mining company more likely to develop first, and why?

options.text_md: Q, because deeper deposits are always richer
Q, because remote deposits cost less to mine
Both equally, because the metal is the same
P, because a richer, shallower deposit near transport makes extraction pay

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Whether a deposit is worth mining depends on its concentration, depth and access.
Step 2: P is four times richer, much shallower and close to a railway, so its ore is far cheaper to extract and move. So (d).

questions.stem_md: An imagined drilling crew drilling down into the crest of an upfold strikes natural gas first and oil a little deeper. Why?

options.text_md: Oil is lighter than gas
Gas is formed only near the surface
Gas is lighter than oil, so it collects above the oil beneath the non-porous cap rock
Oil is always found in granite

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: In an anticline trap, oil and gas collect in porous rock under a non-porous cap.
Step 2: Gas is lighter, so it rises above the oil, and the drill meets it first. So (c).

questions.stem_md: An imagined island in the Bay of Bengal has no coal or oil, strong sunshine for most of the year and a large tidal range in its bays. It imports diesel at high cost. Which energy plan suits it best?

options.text_md: Build a coal-fired plant and import coal
Combine solar power with a tidal plant in a suitable bay, keeping diesel only as back-up
Build a lignite power station
Depend fully on imported diesel

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The island's own resources are sun and tides; fossil fuels must be imported at high cost.
Step 2: Solar and tidal power use local, renewable resources; diesel can cover calm or cloudy gaps. So (b).
Step 3: (a), (c) and (d) rely on fuels the island lacks.

questions.stem_md: An imagined coalfield has reserves of 600 million tonnes and produces 20 million tonnes a year. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: At this rate the reserves will last 30 years; if output doubles, they will last 15 years
At this rate the reserves will last 300 years
The reserves will last for ever because coal is renewable
If output doubles, the reserves will last 60 years

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: 600 ÷ 20 = 30 years.
Step 2: At 40 million tonnes a year, 600 ÷ 40 = 15 years.
Step 3: So (a). (c) is false, since coal is non-renewable; (b) and (d) are miscalculations.

questions.stem_md: Two of India's nuclear power plants, Tarapur and Kalpakkam, are on the coast. Suggest two reasons for such locations.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Nuclear plants need huge amounts of **cooling water**, which the **sea** provides. (ii) Coastal sites can be kept away from **dense inland populations**, and heavy equipment can arrive by **sea**.

questions.solution_md: Cooling water and site factors.

questions.stem_md: Why are thermal power stations often built near coalfields, while hydel stations are built in hilly areas? Explain three points.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Coal is heavy** and leaves much of its weight as ash, so carrying it far is costly; plants sit near **coalfields** such as Singrauli. (ii) Hydel needs **fast-flowing water** and a **head** (height of fall), found in **hills and gorges**. (iii) So each plant goes where its **energy source** is cheapest to use; power travels easily by **transmission lines**.

questions.solution_md: Explain both locations and the common principle.

questions.stem_md: An imagined state has 900 million tonnes of bauxite and mines 30 million tonnes a year. How long will the reserves last at this rate? Suggest two ways to make them last longer.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) 900 ÷ 30 = **30 years** at the present rate. (ii) **Recycle aluminium** cans, foil and scrap, which needs far less new bauxite. (iii) Use better **technology** to process **lower-grade** bauxite, so more of the deposit becomes usable.

questions.solution_md: Calculate, then two conservation measures.
